name: Maridebart cafraglutide
lead: Maridebart cafraglutide, also known as MariTide and formerly AMG 133, is an investigational drug developed by Amgen for obesity and related conditions. It is a long-acting antibody-peptide conjugate: a fully human antibody that blocks the GIP receptor, linked to GLP-1 analogue peptides that activate the GLP-1 receptor. [1][2]

In a phase 2 randomised, placebo-controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine, people with obesity who received the drug by subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks or less often lost between 12.3% and 16.2% of body weight at 52 weeks (treatment-policy estimand), compared with 2.5% on placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were common but less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose, and the investigators reported no unexpected safety signals. [3]

As of late 2026 the drug is not approved by any regulator. It is in phase 3 development under Amgen's MARITIME programme, with registered trials in obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, sleep apnoea and cardiovascular outcomes. [4][5][6][7][8] It is discussed in appearance-focused communities mainly as one of the next-generation injectable weight-loss drugs, because of its monthly or less frequent dosing.
infobox: GLP-1 receptor agonist / GIP receptor antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate

paras: The molecule joins a human monoclonal antibody that antagonises the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor to two GLP-1 analogue peptides through linkers. It therefore activates the GLP-1 receptor while blocking the GIP receptor. [1][3]

This differs from tirzepatide, which activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. The rationale for GIP antagonism, according to reviews, draws on human genetic findings and animal studies in which combining GLP-1 agonism with GIP-receptor blockade produced greater weight loss than either alone. The question of whether GIP receptor agonism or antagonism is the better approach remains a subject of scientific debate. [1][9]

The antibody backbone gives the conjugate a long half-life, which is the basis for monthly or less frequent dosing. Reported preclinical half-lives in rodents and monkeys were in the range of roughly 200 to 300 hours. [1]

The phase 2 trial enrolled 592 adults in two cohorts: 465 with obesity and 127 with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Participants received several dose levels and schedules, with or without dose escalation, or placebo. The primary endpoint was percent change in body weight at week 52. [3]

In the obesity cohort, mean weight change on the treatment-policy estimand ranged from -12.3% to -16.2% across drug arms versus -2.5% with placebo. In the obesity-diabetes cohort it ranged from -8.4% to -12.3% versus -1.7% with placebo, and HbA1c fell by 1.2 to 1.6 percentage points versus 0.1 with placebo. [3] Reviews of the trial note that weight loss had not plateaued at 52 weeks. [1]
Gastrointestinal adverse events were common and were less frequent with dose escalation and a lower starting dose. The authors reported no unexpected safety signals. [3]

Registered phase 3 trials include studies in adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes (3,853 participants planned) [6], in people with type 2 diabetes and obesity [14], a Japanese obesity study [10], a heart failure trial in obesity (5,056) [5], a cardiovascular outcomes trial in atherosclerotic disease (12,800) [7], a sleep apnoea trial [8], long-term extension studies [11][12], and a head-to-head trial against semaglutide in type 2 diabetes [4]. No phase 3 results had been published at the time of writing.

In the phase 2 trial, nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal events were the most frequent adverse events, and were reported as more common without dose escalation. [3] Longer-term safety data will come from the ongoing phase 3 and extension studies. [11][12]

Maridebart cafraglutide is not available outside clinical trials. Amgen positions it among once-monthly obesity candidates; a review of once-monthly incretin, amylin and thyroid-hormone-receptor-beta therapies places it alongside other long-interval agents in development. [13]

timeline.event: Phase 2 results published in the New England Journal of Medicine. [3]
Phase 3 MARITIME trials begin, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure and cardiovascular outcomes studies. [6][5][7]
Extension trials of MARITIME-1 and MARITIME-2 registered. [11][12]

card.summary: Amgen's monthly GLP-1 agonist / GIP-blocker injection, still in phase 3, with roughly 12-16% weight loss at a year in phase 2.
card.note: Investigational and not approved; only available inside clinical trials.

quick.overview:
Maridebart cafraglutide (MariTide) is an experimental injectable obesity drug from Amgen. It is designed to be given monthly or less often, unlike weekly semaglutide or tirzepatide.

In a phase 2 trial of 592 adults, average weight loss at 52 weeks was 12.3% to 16.2% in people with obesity, versus 2.5% on placebo. Large phase 3 trials are under way.
quick.mechanism: It pairs an antibody that blocks the GIP receptor with GLP-1 peptides that activate the GLP-1 receptor. The antibody backbone extends its time in the body, supporting infrequent dosing.
quick.risks: Nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal events were common in phase 2, and less frequent with gradual dose escalation. No unexpected safety signals were reported. It is not approved anywhere, and long-term safety data are still being collected.
